6.3 — Jump Feel: Fall Speed & Coyote Time

Your jump works and your ground check is honest — and the character still feels like it is being operated through a spreadsheet. That is not a vague complaint. "Feel" is four numbers with names, two of them timers that remember a moment, and every platformer you have ever called tight is using all four. Today you learn their names, decide where each one lives, and build the two that are timers.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I make my jump feel good?”Guided build
Break It Down~10 minGuided build

Your jump works and your ground check is honest, and the character still feels like something operated through a spreadsheet: it floats down like a balloon, it refuses a press you made a step past the lip of a ledge, and it throws away a press you made a moment before you landed. "Make my jump feel good" is that whole complaint — and every knob that fixes it is a number somebody chose and wrote down.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Decide which way the body is moving verticallyRead the vertical half of the body's velocity — body.linearVelocity.y in Unity 6, which every tutorial written before it still calls velocity — and the sign is the answer: positive is rising, negative is falling. This is the only part of the lesson that is not about time, and it is the switch the whole fall-speed trick hangs off.Read: the rb.linearVelocity row of the quick reference for the Unity 6 rename, and the submarine example in 6.1, which reads one half of a velocity and overwrites the other.
  2. Make the fall heavier than the riseWrite a bigger gravity multiplier onto the body while it is falling and the body's own value back while it is rising — gravityScale, on the physics clock, every physics step. The "normal" number is read off the body once in Start(), so the Inspector keeps ownership of it.Read: the rb.gravityScale row of the quick reference, and the Gravity Scale table you read in 6.1.
  3. write this partRead: the Time.time row of the quick reference — the clock that only ever counts up — and the field the turret stamped on every shot in 3.3. The reading for "is that moment still recent enough?" is the same three pieces with the operator turned around.
  4. Spend the remembered moment the instant the jump uses itA window that is never closed can be used again on the very next frame. When the jump fires, overwrite the remembered moment with a value so far in the past that no subtraction can bring it back inside the window — the same stamp line as 3.3, written with a different value and for the opposite reason.Read: the Cooldown row of the pattern table (act, set last = Time.time) and your own stamp line from 3.3 — then ask why that line cannot close this window by itself.
  5. Gate the jump on two windows instead of on the groundA press is on file and the body is either standing on something or still inside the grace window. && and || in one condition, and the only line in the file that launches anything.Read: the && you combined the turret's range and cooldown checks with in 3.3, and the isGrounded bool your own 6.2 check produces.
  6. Cut the rise when the key comes back upThe fourth number, and the smallest change of the four: while the body is still rising, the player's release multiplies the upward velocity down, so the rise can be shortened after it has started. The release becomes an input, not just the press.Read: the hold-longer-go-higher row of 6.1's four-technique table, and the rb.linearVelocity row of the quick reference for writing a velocity back to the body.

Four of those six parts are things you have already typed. Reading one half of a velocity is the submarine in 6.1; putting a gravity multiplier on a body is the Gravity Scale field you turned on in 6.1; a key that is true on exactly one frame is 6.1's jump check; and cutting a rise is the hold-longer-go-higher row of 6.1's four-technique table. What is left is the timer, and it is why this lesson is a guided build rather than a full walkthrough. Every memory this game has kept so far was kept for good — a coin count, health, which end of a beat an enemy is walking toward, the moment of the turret's last shot. This memory is different in two ways at once: it is only meant to be true for a fraction of a second, and it has to be thrown away on purpose the moment it is used. A memory you are supposed to forget is a genuinely new shape, and it is the smallest part of the six.

The test: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Make my jump feel good" cannot be looked up — it is four unrelated numbers with two of them being timers. "Compare a timestamp against the clock with a tolerance" can, and you have already written that subtraction once, in 3.3.

Your turn

Two of the four numbers are windows measured in seconds and two are multipliers. Which half of that split would you hand to a teammate as a spreadsheet, and which half do they have to feel for themselves?

Coyote time and the jump buffer both let a press count when a strict reading of the rules says it should not. Pick the one you would set longer than the other, and say what the player would think had gone wrong if you set it to zero.

The Problem: It Works and It Feels Bad ~15 min

Play your cave for thirty seconds and pay attention to your hands, not the screen. Three specific complaints come up — they are the three every playtester in the world reports, and each one is a missing number rather than a missing feature:

  • "I float down like a balloon." Your rise and your fall use the same gravity. Gravity is a real constant and your character is not a real object, so the same number is doing two jobs that want different answers.
  • "It ate my jump at the ledge." The ground check you built in 6.2 turns false on the frame your feet leave the tile. A press made one step past the lip is refused — and the player is certain they jumped.
  • "It ignored my press just before I landed." The mirror image. The press arrives while you are still airborne, nothing is listening, and by the time the ground arrives the input is gone.

The last two are the same problem seen from two sides: a jump that is only accepted at the exact instant the ground check agrees is a jump that rejects the player's intent almost every time it matters. Both fixes are timers, and both of them remember a moment rather than counting anything.

The knobThe complaint it killsWhat it really is
Asymmetric gravity (a fall multiplier) "It floats." One gravity value while the body is rising and a larger one while it is falling, chosen by the sign of its vertical velocity. A multiplier, not a second gravity number.
Coyote time "The ledge ate my jump." Remember the last moment your feet were on something, and keep accepting a jump for a short window after that moment has passed.
Jump buffer "I pressed too early." Remember the last moment the key went down, and fire the jump the instant the ground arrives — if the press was recent enough.
Variable jump height "I can't do small hops." Release the key early and the rise is cut short. The player's release becomes an input, not only their press.
Both mercies are the same subtraction you met in 3.3, read in the opposite direction. The turret wrote a moment into a field and asked "has enough time passed?" — Time.time >= lastAttackTime + cooldown. Coyote time and the buffer ask "has too little passed?" — the same clock, the same remembered moment, the same knob, with the comparison turned around. The three pieces are identical; only the question changed.
A window is not a countdown — pick one idiom per field. 3.3 named both honest timers: a timestamp compared against Time.time, and a countdown with Time.deltaTime subtracted from it every frame. Both work. What does not work is one field doing both jobs: a number that means "when it happened" on the frame you write it and "how long is left" everywhere else has no correct comparison, and the bug looks like the window closing at the wrong moment. Today's two fields are both timestamps, because both of them answer questions about when.

Socratic: Forgiving Intent Versus Playing For Them

  1. Coyote time and the jump buffer both let a press count when it "should not". Why does that make the player feel more in control, when technically it makes the game more permissive?
  2. Set coyote time long enough and you can jump from thin air a metre past a ledge. What is the difference between forgiving the player's intent and playing the game for them?
  3. Asymmetric gravity is a lie about physics, told by a multiplier on a law of the universe. What other lie does your character already tell — and what does each lie buy the player?
  4. Which of the four knobs needs to know which way the body is moving, and which of them only need to know about time?
Read Function-Level Examples ~10 min

Each of these is a timer with a name, from somewhere that is not a video game. Read it for the shape of the logic, then decide which of your four knobs it describes. Two of them print a line of code, because the shape is the thing worth seeing.

Example 1 — A subway door that stays open a moment longer (comment only):

// The doors do not reopen because a hand is in them. They reopen because the
// hand was in them a fraction of a second ago and the timer has not expired.

Example 2 — A parking meter grace period:

bool stillFine = Time.time - paidAt <= gracePeriod; // paid a moment ago, not now

Example 3 — A lift that reopens if you press within a second (comment only):

// The press is remembered, not honoured immediately. The doors are already
// closing; the remembered press is what brings them back.

Example 4 — A wind tunnel ramping down instead of cutting off:

// Falling air is not the same as rising air. The tunnel is symmetric on paper
// and asymmetric in the test chamber, on purpose.

Example 5 — A keyboard's repeat delay:

// Hold the key and the characters start after a pause, then arrive fast.
// The pause is a number somebody chose.

Map Them Before You Build Them

  1. Which example is coyote time, and which is the jump buffer? Be precise — one of them remembers a state and one remembers a press.
  2. The lift example remembers a press that arrives too late. In your game, what is the equivalent of "the doors are already closing"?
  3. The wind tunnel is asymmetric on purpose. Which of your two directions should be the strong one, and what does the player read into that?
Build It With MeGuided build

The question this answers“how do I make my jump feel good?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs. Four numbers, one gravity line on the physics clock, and two fields that hold a moment in time. The fall multiplier is arithmetic on a value you already read; the two mercies are the timestamp pattern from 3.3 run twice, and one of the two windows is yours to write. Your launch from 6.1 and your ground check from 6.2 are not touched.

This build leaves 1 line for you to write. Everything around it is given, so you always know the shape of what you are producing.

Step 1Declare the four numbers, and the two moments they are measured against

Seven lines in the class body, beside moveSpeed and your jump force. Four of them are knobs a designer turns and the other three are this script's own bookkeeping — the same split as range and lastAttackTime on the turret in 3.3.

    [SerializeField] private float fallMultiplier = 2.5f;
    [SerializeField] private float riseCut = 0.5f;
    [SerializeField] private float coyoteTime = 0.1f;
    [SerializeField] private float jumpBufferTime = 0.12f;
    private float lastGroundedTime;
    private float lastJumpPressedTime;
    private float baseGravity;

    // ... the distance and the mask your 6.2 ground check already uses ...
  1. 1The fall-speed knob. A multiplier on the body's own gravity, applied only while it is falling. 1 is the balloon you have now, 2.5 is what most platformers use, 3 starts to read as heavy.A multiplier, not a gravity value. The cave's Gravity Scale is a number that lives on the body — a scene instance, the prefab, or a line in Start(), depending on what you chose in 6.1. Type 9 here and you now own two gravity numbers that have to agree; the day either one changes, the jump is quietly wrong. A multiplier cannot disagree with anything.
  2. 2The fourth number. How much of the rise survives when the player lets go of the key — 0.5 halves it. 1 switches the knob off entirely, which is where your game is now.
  3. 3The grace window, in seconds. How long after your feet leave the ground a jump is still accepted. A tenth of a second is about six frames in the cave — roughly the width of the mistake a player makes at the lip of a ledge.Seconds, not frames. A frame counter means six frames on your machine and six frames on a laptop running at half the speed, which is a different amount of time and therefore a different game. Time.time counts seconds on every machine, so the window you tuned is the window everybody gets.
  4. 4How long a press is remembered, in seconds. A jump pressed this recently is still valid once the ground arrives.Slightly longer than the coyote window, and for a reason. A player who presses early is watching their landing, so their timing error tends to be bigger than the one at a ledge. The two are separate knobs on purpose — tune them apart and find out whether that is true for you.
  5. 5The first memory. The moment, on the game clock, when the feet were last known to be on something. private, because it is this script's own bookkeeping and no other file has business reading it — the same declaration, for the same reason, as the turret's lastAttackTime.Notice that it has no value yet — step 3 gives it one. And notice where it lives: the class body, not inside Update(). A variable declared inside a method is built fresh every time that method runs, so a timestamp kept in there would be rebuilt from nothing sixty times a second and could never remember anything at all. That is the scope rule from 1.3, and the identical mistake would break lastAttackTime in 3.3.
  6. 6The second memory. The moment the jump key was last pressed down. Deliberately a separate field from the one above: two timers, two names, two jobs, and nothing shared between them.
  7. 7Where the "normal" gravity is kept. It is read off the body once, in Start(), so the multiplier has something honest to multiply — and so the Inspector keeps ownership of the real number.A private field rather than a second serialized knob. Give the multiplier its own baseGravity slot in the Inspector and a teammate can set the two numbers against each other until the cave's gravity means nothing. Reading it off the body means the two can never drift.
  8. 9Untouched. Whatever fields your check needs are already declared beside it, and they stay exactly where they are — this file asks the check a question in step 3, it does not change it.

Step 2Make the fall heavier than the rise

One branch, on the physics clock, in FixedUpdate(). It reads the body's vertical velocity and hands the body a gravity scale — and that is the whole of the "it floats" complaint.

    void FixedUpdate()
    {
        if (body.linearVelocity.y < 0f)
        {
            body.gravityScale = baseGravity * fallMultiplier;
        }
        else
        {
            body.gravityScale = baseGravity;
        }
    }
  1. 1The physics step — the method your 6.2 ground check was argued onto. gravityScale is a property the physics engine reads, so it belongs on the clock the physics engine runs on.FixedUpdate() and not Update(). FixedUpdate runs on the physics clock: fifty times a second in this project (Fixed Timestep 0.02), whatever rate the machine is drawing frames at. Gravity is applied by the physics engine, on that clock, so the value it reads should be written there too — on a 144 Hz monitor Update() runs about three times per physics step and writes the same number three times for nothing.
  2. 3The switch, and the only line in this lesson that is about direction instead of time. linearVelocity is the body's velocity as a Vector2; .y is the vertical half; below zero means the body is on its way down.Read it, never re-derive it. The sign of the velocity is the engine's own answer to "am I falling", and it is already correct — on the way up after a jump it is positive even though gravity is pulling the whole time. A boolean of your own would have to be set true and false in the right places, and the frame it is wrong is a frame where the fall speed is wrong.
  3. 5The fall is now heavier. Notice what is not on this line: no Time.deltaTime, no Time.fixedDeltaTime. Gravity Scale is a multiplier, not a rate, so time is not part of it anywhere.Multiply, never add. baseGravity + fallMultiplier looks plausible at 2.5 and is nonsense the moment somebody sets the knob to 0.5 — and the day the cave's gravity is retuned from 1 to 3, the additive version silently changes what your knob means.
  4. 9The branch everybody leaves out. While the body is rising — and while it is standing still, and on the very first frame after a jump — gravity goes back to the body's own value.Without this line the multiplier is permanent. Write only the falling branch and gravity never returns to normal, so the rise is crushed by the heavy fall gravity: the first jump looks fine and every jump after it barely leaves the floor. It is worth building exactly that once, on purpose, and watching it happen.
  5. 11Closes FixedUpdate(). Your Update() is still the only place anything else happens.

Step 3Remember where you last stood — and write the window that reads it back

Two given lines and one gap. The line that writes the moment down is the turret's stamp from 3.3; the line you write is the same subtraction with the question turned around.

        if (isGrounded)
        {
            lastGroundedTime = Time.time;
        }
        bool stillInGrace = ______________________________________;
  1. 1Where the memory is written. isGrounded is the bool your 6.2 check leaves behind — and this block is the only place it is read for this purpose, because a second ground check in this file would be a second answer to the same question and one of them would be wrong.One ground check, one place. If your 6.2 check lives in a method of its own, this block goes directly underneath the call that runs it. Record the moment anywhere else and the file now asks "am I standing on something?" twice, with nothing keeping the two answers in step.
  2. 3The memory, refreshed on every frame the feet are down. This is 3.3's stamp line — the clock that only ever counts up, written down at the moment the interesting thing happened. What is interesting today is "still standing on something".A moment, not a countdown. 3.3 named both honest timers: a timestamp compared against Time.time, and a field with Time.deltaTime subtracted from it until it reaches zero. Both work — but not in the same field. A timestamp is compared against the clock; a countdown is decremented. One number with two meanings has neither behaviour.
  3. Your turn5Your line — the whole right-hand side. It answers one question: is the moment you just wrote down still recent enough to count as standing? The declaration on the left is fixed — stillInGrace is the name step 4 consumes, so do not rename it — and everything from the = onward is yours to work out.Three pieces go into it. One is the moment you recorded on the line above; one is the window you declared as a knob in step 1; and the third is the clock that only ever counts up — the row of the quick reference whose description is the seconds since the scene started, which is the same row the turret stamped on every shot in 3.3. Put all three into one comparison, and then ask which way round it has to run: 3.3 asked whether enough time had passed, and this one asks the mirror question. == is exactly as wrong here as it was there.The same subtraction, read backwards. 3.3 asked clock >= moment + gap. This asks whether too little time has passed — same three pieces, same subtraction, opposite operator, and the answer is a bool rather than a jump. Keeping it in a named bool is what lets step 4 ask about standing and about pressing in the same breath.

Step 4Remember the last press, and open the gate that uses both

The mirror of step 3, written by the key instead of by the floor. Then one condition that needs both memories to be true, and one call.

        if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space))
        {
            lastJumpPressedTime = Time.time;
        }
        bool pressedRecently = Time.time - lastJumpPressedTime <= jumpBufferTime;

        if (pressedRecently && (isGrounded || stillInGrace))
        {
            Jump();
        }
  1. 1The single-frame key check from 6.1 — true on exactly one frame. It is not the jump; it is only the moment being written down.This line could not sit inside the jump condition any more, and that is the whole of the buffer. In 6.2 the key check was the second half of if (isGrounded && Input.GetKeyDown(...)) — a press was only ever considered while you were standing on something, so a press made in mid-air was not rejected, it was never seen at all. Here the press is written down first and judged afterwards, which is exactly what makes remembering it possible. And GetKey would refresh the memory every frame the key is held: lean on the jump key and you would have a press on file for as long as you held it, so the buffer would fire the instant you touched the floor, from a press made seconds earlier. The one-frame version is the whole point of a press.
  2. 3The same stamp, on the other field. If it looks like the line above, that is the lesson: two timers, written by two different events, read by two different questions.
  3. 5The buffer's window — the line you wrote in step 3, with the other field and the other knob in it. Nothing about the shape changed, which is exactly why step 3 asked you to produce it.Two windows, two knobs, two fields. Sharing one field between them would make the grace at a ledge and the grace before a landing the same length. That sounds tidy and is not: they forgive mistakes of different sizes, made in opposite directions.
  4. 7The gate, and the only line in the file that launches anything. Read it as a sentence: a press is on file, and the body is either standing on something or still inside the grace window.This is the line that keeps two mercies from becoming a jetpack. Drop stillInGrace and you have 6.2's plain ground check — correct, and it refuses the press a player made one step past the lip. Drop pressedRecently and the jump fires the instant you touch down whether or not anybody asked for it. Drop the isGrounded half and you can jump from anywhere at all, which is a different lesson and a worse game.
  5. 9The method from 6.1, called from exactly one place — and that place now has a rule about when. Whatever your launch is — an impulse, a velocity assignment, the row you chose in 6.1 — nothing about it changes today except the company it keeps.

Step 5Spend both windows the moment the jump fires

Two lines, and they are the difference between a mercy and a jetpack. Without them the window you just used is still open on the next frame.

        body.AddForce(Vector2.up * jumpForce, ForceMode2D.Impulse);
        lastGroundedTime = -999f;
        lastJumpPressedTime = -999f;
    }
  1. 1Your launch from 6.1, unchanged — the same flick you wrote there, one line, and nothing about it changes today. If you picked one of the other Dynamic-body rows instead (writing linearVelocity directly), keep that one: it is the same jump by a different route, and nothing else in this file cares which you chose.One of 6.1's four rows cannot be used with this lesson at all. MovePosition() on a Kinematic body: a Kinematic body ignores gravity, so it never falls — which means there is no velocity for the heavy branch to read and no gravity for it to fight. Both AddForce rows and the direct linearVelocity row need a Dynamic body with Gravity Scale above 0, and that is the premise this entire page is built on. If the Kinematic row is the one you wrote in 6.1, switch it now: it is one line, and this is the last moment before the fall multiplier has nothing to act on.
  2. 2The spend, and the new idea in this lesson. A moment far enough in the past that no subtraction can ever bring it back inside the window. The jump you just made has used the grace up; the next frame must not be able to use it again.Why not -coyoteTime, the way 3.3 seeded its turret? Because the question is different. 3.3 asked "has enough time passed since last", and pushing last back by one cooldown made that true — the gate closed itself. This window asks whether too little has passed, so pushing the moment back by exactly one window leaves it sitting on the boundary, ready to open the gate again on frame one. A value far in the past cannot do that.
  3. 3The same spend, on the other window. Both have to be closed: the press you just honoured must not be honoured again when you leave the ground, and the grace you just used must not survive into the next frame.
  4. 4Closes the jump. One more } closes the class.

Step 6The fourth number: cut the rise when the key comes back up

Three lines, and the player's release becomes an input for the first time. Press for a full jump, tap for a small one.

        if (Input.GetKeyUp(KeyCode.Space) && body.linearVelocity.y > 0f)
        {
            body.linearVelocity = new Vector2(body.linearVelocity.x, body.linearVelocity.y * riseCut);
        }
  1. 1The key coming up, and the body still rising. Two conditions, because a release while you are already falling must not do anything — there is no rise left to cut.GetKeyUp is the third key question this course has asked. GetKey is a state, GetKeyDown is a press, GetKeyUp is the release — the same three shapes you met on the mouse in 1.6, and choosing the wrong one is invisible in the code and obvious in the hands. One edge case falls straight out of 6.1's own proof: AddForce does not change linearVelocity until the physics engine next runs, so a player who presses and releases inside a single frame lets go before the rise exists. There is nothing to cut, nothing errors — and it is why this line asks the body whether it is rising instead of assuming a jump has just happened.
  2. 3Multiply the upward half of the velocity down instead of setting it to zero. A hard 0 kills the rise dead and reads as a collision; a multiplier reads as the character choosing to come down.This is where the buffer and the rise cut can collide. A buffered jump fires the instant you land, from a press made before the landing — and if the player has already released the key, this block cuts that jump on its very first frame, so a buffered jump arrives already half spent. Test the two together before you decide the numbers.

Step 7Wire the four numbers, then prove each one is real

No code in this step. Every number you declared has an Inspector row, and every one of them has a behaviour you can watch — separately.

// Assets/Prefabs/Player ▸ PlayerController ▸ Fall Multiplier = 1
// ... then 2.5, then 3
// Coyote Time = 0.1, then 0.5
// Jump Buffer Time = 0.12, then 1
// Rise Cut = 0.5, then 0
// Prove the windows are state, not luck
  1. 1Set it to 1 first, before any of the others. That is the balloon you started with, and it is your control: if the jump does not feel exactly as bad as it did yesterday, something other than this lesson changed.
  2. 2One number at a time, one sentence of feel written down for each. The fall multiplier is the only one of the four whose effect the player feels on every jump without doing anything — it is the cheapest of the four to test.
  3. 3Walk off a ledge and press jump as late as you dare. At 0.1 it forgives the mistake a person actually makes; at 0.5 you can leave a ledge, decide about it, and jump anyway — which is the difference between forgiving an intent and playing the game for them.
  4. 4Press jump a fraction of a second before you land. At 0.12 the landing honours the press; at 1 a press made a full second early still fires, and every fall becomes a jump you did not ask for.
  5. 5Tap the key and then hold it, side by side. 0.5 gives two visibly different jumps; 0 gives a tap that does nothing at all, which is a bug rather than a mechanic.
  6. 6Add Debug.Log("grounded at " + lastGroundedTime + " now " + Time.time); for one run and watch the two numbers while you walk off a ledge and land. The gap between them is your coyote window, live. Then delete the print — Update() runs sixty times a second and a log that survives into the next lesson is noise you will be reading past.
Check your work: the finished filetry every gap first — then open this to compare

Compare against your own file rather than copying it. Three things have to match and nothing else does: the fall multiplier is written on the physics clock and restored on the way up, the jump is gated by two windows rather than by the ground check alone, and both windows are spent the instant the jump fires. The gap is the coyote window, and this file writes it as a subtraction against the clock with <= — a window is a length of time, so the question is whether the time since that moment is still shorter than the knob, which is the mirror of the >= 3.3 used. Your launch from 6.1, your ground check from 6.2, your names and all four of your numbers are yours.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;

// PlayerController.cs — the jump, and the four numbers that make it feel like
// yours. Movement 1.4, animation 1.6, the velocity rule 2.2, the launch from
// 6.1, the ground check from 6.2 — and the two mercies.
public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private float moveSpeed = 5f;
    [SerializeField] private float jumpForce = 7f;          // yours already — 6.1's step 1

    // ---- the four numbers this lesson is about --------------------------
    [SerializeField] private float fallMultiplier = 2.5f;   // heavier going down
    [SerializeField] private float riseCut = 0.5f;          // release shortens the rise
    [SerializeField] private float coyoteTime = 0.1f;       // grace after the ledge
    [SerializeField] private float jumpBufferTime = 0.12f;  // grace before the floor

    // ---- your 6.2 check, unchanged. This file writes the raycast row; if you
    // picked a different one, CheckGround() is the only place that changes. ---
    [SerializeField] private float groundDistance = 0.6f;
    [SerializeField] private LayerMask groundMask;

    private Rigidbody2D body;
    private float baseGravity;          // read once, so the Inspector still owns it

    private bool isGrounded;
    private float lastGroundedTime;     // a MOMENT, not a count
    private float lastJumpPressedTime;  // the other moment, a different field

    void Start()
    {
        body = GetComponent<Rigidbody2D>();

        // ... your 6.1 gravity line, if you wrote one for the scene ...
        baseGravity = body.gravityScale;    // read it LAST — after your 6.1 gravity line above
    }

    void Update()
    {
        // ... your input, movement and animation from 1.4, 1.6 and 2.2 ...
        CheckGround();

        // The memory: refreshed on every frame the feet are down.
        if (isGrounded)
        {
            lastGroundedTime = Time.time;
        }

        // The other memory: written by the key, on the frame it goes down.
        if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space))
        {
            lastJumpPressedTime = Time.time;
        }

        // The same subtraction twice, asked in opposite directions.
        bool stillInGrace = Time.time - lastGroundedTime <= coyoteTime;
        bool pressedRecently = Time.time - lastJumpPressedTime <= jumpBufferTime;

        if (pressedRecently && (isGrounded || stillInGrace))
        {
            Jump();
        }

        // The fourth number: let go early and the rise is cut short.
        if (Input.GetKeyUp(KeyCode.Space) && body.linearVelocity.y > 0f)
        {
            body.linearVelocity = new Vector2(body.linearVelocity.x, body.linearVelocity.y * riseCut);
        }
    }

    // Gravity is a value the physics engine reads, so it is written on the
    // physics clock: fifty times a second here, whatever the frame rate is.
    void FixedUpdate()
    {
        if (body.linearVelocity.y < 0f)
        {
            body.gravityScale = baseGravity * fallMultiplier;
        }
        else
        {
            body.gravityScale = baseGravity;
        }
    }

    private void Jump()
    {
        // Your launch from 6.1: one flick. Writing linearVelocity directly
        // works identically here — the Kinematic MovePosition row does not,
        // because a Kinematic body has no gravity for the fall branch to fight.
        body.AddForce(Vector2.up * jumpForce, ForceMode2D.Impulse);

        // Spend both windows. A window that is never closed is a jetpack —
        // and unlike the turret's cooldown, this one cannot close itself.
        lastGroundedTime = -999f;
        lastJumpPressedTime = -999f;
    }

    private void CheckGround()
    {
        // A RaycastHit2D is true when the ray hit something and false when it
        // did not, so it stores straight into the bool. Your 6.2 technique,
        // whichever of the four you chose, belongs on this line.
        isGrounded = Physics2D.Raycast(transform.position, Vector2.down, groundDistance, groundMask);
    }
}

// Inspector, on Assets/Prefabs/Player ▸ PlayerController:
//   Fall Multiplier    =  2.5     <- 1 is the balloon you started with
//   Rise Cut           =  0.5     <- 1 switches the fourth knob off
//   Coyote Time        =  0.1     <- about six frames in the cave
//   Jump Buffer Time   =  0.12    <- how long a press is remembered
//   Ground Distance    =  measured, not guessed (6.2)
//   Ground Mask        =  Ground  <- the layer you created in 6.2
Build Lab: Tune the Four Numbers ~30 min

The walkthrough built the reference version of all four. What it cannot give you is the numbers, because they are the design — and every one of them is now an Inspector row. Below are the decisions a spec cannot make for you.

Architectural specification: the fall multiplier.
  • Where does the "normal" gravity number live in your project — a literal in your own code, a serialized field, a scene-instance value, or a value you read off the body? Whatever the answer, you now need it in a second place, and that is a design smell worth fixing rather than living with.
  • Is the value you multiply your own field or the body's gravityScale? Which choice survives a teammate retuning the cave in the Inspector, and which survives a teammate changing the scene-mode logic you wrote in 6.1?
  • What happens in the top-down Overworld if this branch runs there? Before you answer, look at the Player in that scene. The two scenes are separate instances of the same prefab, and a scene can still be holding a setting for a component the prefab no longer has — so check the Gravity Scale that is actually there rather than the one you remember setting. Whatever you find, the restore line is what keeps this branch from changing it: baseGravity was read off the body once, so the multiply and the restore can only ever be a round trip.
  • Which scene-mode decision from 6.1 gates this branch, and does the branch need to be gated at all if the restore is written correctly? Try it ungated and describe what the Overworld does.
Architectural specification: the two mercies.
  • What exact moment does each field record, and which event writes it? Say it in one sentence per field, and use the word "moment" in both, not "timer".
  • How long is each window, in seconds? Write your two numbers down beside a sentence of feel for each, the way you did for the jump force in 6.1.
  • What is the "spend" rule — and can the same jump fire twice off one remembered press if you get it wrong? Which of the two windows does the double-fire actually come from?
  • What is the initial value of each field before anything has ever happened — before the player's feet have touched the ground, and before the key has ever been pressed? If it starts at 0 and the scene clock also starts near 0, what does your first frame of play do?
  • Do the two windows use the same comparison operator as each other, and is that the operator you meant? Say which way the boundary falls for a player standing exactly on it.
Architectural specification: the fourth number.
  • What does the release actually cut — the whole velocity, or a fraction of it? Which of the two reads as a decision by the character rather than as a collision?
  • When is the cut allowed? Only while rising, or on the way down too? What would a cut on the way down even mean for a player who is falling?
  • How does the cut interact with a buffered jump the player never held? Describe the two knobs fighting, then decide which one you would weaken.
  • If you chose the impulse row in 6.1 rather than the velocity row: does cutting linearVelocity still work, and why? What is it about the body that makes the answer yes?
Two timers and one jump key is how you build an infinite jump by accident. Watch the Console line you print each time the jump fires. If the count climbs while you are nowhere near the floor, one of the two remembered moments is being refreshed when it should not be — or one of them is not being spent. Note that 3.3's cooldown could never fail this way: its gate closed itself the moment it fired, and a window read backwards does not.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain asymmetric gravity as a multiplier on the body's own value, and apply it on the physics clock
  • Say where the "normal" gravity number lives, and why multiplying it beats storing a second copy
  • Build coyote time and the jump buffer from the timestamp pattern in 3.3, and say which way the comparison turned
  • Explain "spending" a window, and why a window read backwards cannot close itself the way a cooldown does
  • Defend all four knobs as intent-forgiveness rather than difficulty-lowering
  • Commit and push
